field_diffs.before: Public oath requirements and replacement of refusers force political alignment; only 109 clerical deputies and two bishops comply.
field_diffs.after: The public post-Mass oath to nation, king, law and constitution requires replacement of refusers; only 109 clerical deputies and two episcopal deputies comply. Roughly half the wider clergy resist amid pressure, and compelled choice paradoxically recognizes and legitimizes dissent.

field_diffs.before: Regional differences, parish solidarity and lay pressure explain why about 54 percent of parish clergy swear; the result also indicates wider public limits to support.
field_diffs.after: High acceptance near Paris, in the Pyrenees and in the southeast contrasts with several culturally distinct borderlands, areas of Protestant conflict and especially the west. Western priests’ local peasant origins and parish solidarity matter alongside income, clubs, officials and lay pressure. About 54 percent of parish clergy swear; the author infers a much wider constituency setting limits to revolution, not an exact national plebiscite.

field_diffs.before: Cordeliers and popular societies encourage mobilization independently of the Jacobin constitutional programme.
field_diffs.after: Cordeliers and popular societies organize around rights rather than fidelity to the existing constitution, encouraging anti-royal and anti-clerical mobilization independently of the Jacobin programme.

field_diffs.before: The Cordeliers petition demands deposition or consultation of the nation after Varennes.
field_diffs.after: After Varennes, attacks on royal symbols accompany popular reaction; the Cordeliers separately present a mass-supported petition demanding deposition or consultation of the nation.

field_diffs.before: The Social Circle publicizes and organizes pressure for a joint anti-restoration petition.
field_diffs.after: The Social Circle publicizes the Cordeliers petition and brings thousands to press the Jacobins for a joint campaign against royal reinstatement.

field_diffs.before: Brissot’s press and Social Circle activity explain his democratic reputation; the Cordeliers proceed after Jacobin withdrawal, then repression ends the Circle and halts Cordeliers activity.
field_diffs.after: The Social Circle’s newspaper issues the anti-restoration petition; the Cordeliers proceed after Jacobin withdrawal. Repression after the massacre ends the Circle permanently and halts Cordeliers activity, while Brissot’s press and Circle work explain his democratic reputation.

The Commons refuses separate verification while nobles constitute separately and clergy narrowly choose separate verification.

after.evidence_summary: The nobility completes separate verification by a large majority, while clerical hesitation and the Commons’ insistence on joint verification prolong the procedural deadlock.

field_diffs.before: Rights, National Guard and paper money illustrate outcomes beyond cahiers; broad participation and consensus sustain change.
field_diffs.after: Rights, National Guard and paper money illustrate outcomes beyond the cahiers; broad approval, participation and communal celebration sustain unprecedented reconstruction before the consensus rapidly fractures.

field_diffs.before: On 1 August the Assembly orders émigrés to return under threat of triple taxation and begins official lists.
field_diffs.after: On 1 August the Assembly orders émigrés to return under threat of triple taxation and begins official lists; the king also urges Artois to return.

field_diffs.before: The new military oath and Varennes provoke an estimated six thousand officer departures; September repeal and amnesty fail to halt the flow.
field_diffs.after: The new loyalty oath and Varennes provoke an estimated six thousand officer departures, over half the corps; collapse of trust and renewed mutinies push even reluctant officers out. September repeal and amnesty fail to halt the flow.

field_diffs.before: National Guard federations expand into a national celebration involving the king and religious ceremony.
field_diffs.after: National Guard federations culminate in mass oath-taking on the Champ de Mars with the king and religious ceremony, amid genuine optimism about constitutional achievements.

field_diffs.before: Paris administrative reorganization replaces the sixty electoral districts with forty-eight sections; Cordeliers resistance and Danton illustrate local political autonomy.
field_diffs.after: Sixty Paris districts are replaced by forty-eight sections partly to restrain radicalism; Danton’s Cordeliers organization and allied newspapers resist, then retain local dominance in the Théâtre-Français section.

field_diffs.before: Existing indirect levies are abolished and collection problems persist.
field_diffs.after: Organized resistance and nonpayment sharply reduce old indirect-tax receipts and persist while the Assembly abolishes levies and designs an equal system.

field_diffs.before: Legal abolition distinguishes uncompensated personal burdens from redeemable dues and makes sweeping changes to privilege and tithes.
field_diffs.after: Legal abolition distinguishes uncompensated personal burdens and tithes from redeemable seigneurial dues, which remain payable pending compensation; widespread peasant refusal makes the settlement ineffective in practice.

field_diffs.before: Resistance continues despite the formal redemption settlement.
field_diffs.after: Detailed redemption rules reinforce legislators’ resolve to protect compensable rights but fail to overcome rural refusal and ineffective local enforcement.

field_diffs.before: The queen was not involved in the necklace fraud, but the trial, acquittal, public celebration and royal response deepened court disrepute.
field_diffs.after: Royal-marriage ridicule and the queen’s spending, Austrian ties and interventions fed hostility. Rohan’s attempt to gain favour led him into a fraud in which the queen was uninvolved; trial, acquittal, public celebration and his exile deepened Court disrepute. The king’s esteem had partly recovered, while disclosure of Court costs in 1787 reinforced reputational damage.

before.evidence_summary: The Paris parlement's qualified retreat preserves the ancient judicial districts as the relevant 1614 feature.
The January regulations, territorial units, urban and provincial exceptions, and separate order assemblies are explained in detail.
The regulations define district groupings, exceptional provinces, order assemblies, suffrage, delegate stages, and the two-two-four allocation.
The January rules group smaller districts, grant some towns separate representation, and add districts after petitions.
Dauphine and Navarre retain estate-based election, while Brittany's conflict produces separate arrangements for its orders.
They require cahiers and structure a nationwide but socially filtered process.
Judges from these courts later constitute a major segment of third-estate deputies.
The resulting delegation strongly favors legal professionals and officeholders.
Every male taxpayer over twenty-five could attend a primary assembly, which chose delegates to the final electoral assembly.
Formal primary eligibility is broad, but the third estate must elect delegates before ultimate deputies are chosen.
Indirect procedure allows widespread grievance participation while excluding those without leisure from deputy selection.
Indirect voting and lack of leisure remove peasants, artisans, and many poorer citizens before deputy selection.
The rules effectively excluded peasants, artisans, and those unable to spare time for the later stage.
No peasants or artisans pass beyond the first stage, and even eligible Paris voters participate selectively.
Even at the first stage many eligible voters abstain and favor socially similar representatives.
Costs and skill requirements help produce a delegation dominated by lawyers and officeholders.
The chapter explicitly distinguishes ministerial noninterference from the powerful compositional effects of the regulations.
Necker declines serious interference, yet the rules empower parish priests, swamp former noble leaders, and eliminate poorer groups from final selection.
Parish priests' overwhelming success illustrates the displacement of established ecclesiastical corporations.
The resulting third-estate delegation reflects structural advantages for legally trained and officeholding participants.
Cahier drafting drew public affairs beyond major cities and is characterized as an unprecedented democratic spectacle.
Cahier drafting reaches communities across the country and creates unprecedented participation.
The drafting process draws the whole country into articulated grievances and aspirations and is judged unprecedented in Europe.
Election meetings nevertheless interact with economic rumor and popular disorder.
Order-specific electoral outcomes overturn established leadership in clergy and nobility.
Low turnout and the preference for educated candidates narrowed the initial breadth of the franchise.
Only a minority exercises the primary vote in Paris, and participants tend to choose educated men like themselves.
The final third-estate delegation was homogeneous, legally trained, and united despite the wide initial electorate.
The final social composition shows how mass participation narrowed into professional representation.
The electoral rules give parish clergy numerical weight over ecclesiastical corporations.
Three-quarters of clerical deputies were parish priests; their reform grievances coexisted with a strong program for Catholic institutional authority.
Three-quarters of clerical deputies are parish priests, and their cahiers demand stipends, access to office, and elected synods.
Clerical reform demands coexist with broad agreement on education, censorship, Catholic authority, and restricted Protestant rights.
The text stresses that this deeper unity outweighed disagreements about parish-priest status, though contemporaries largely missed it.
The clerical order narrowly accepts separate verification but refuses to constitute itself fully, seeking compromise.
Parish priests begin crossing to common verification.
Most remaining clergy join the National Assembly after royal enforcement fails.
Court and robe elites encounter rejection in noble elections.
Provincial families predominate; voting preferences and liberal-intransigent divisions reveal fragmentation, with both camps socially diverse.
The indirect system removes those without leisure before final selection.
Peasants and artisans disappeared after the first stage, while education, leisure, and speaking experience became practical qualifications.
Primary voters favor educated men like themselves and final deputies must meet expenses.
Legal professionals and officeholders dominated the final group, which shared equality and vote-by-head commitments.
Legal qualifications and venal offices overwhelmingly outnumber deputies from trade or industry.
Most third-estate deputies are locally known rather than national leaders, but shared background and equality commitments unite them.
They refuse separate verification because it would preserve order voting.
A large majority backs Sieyes's final appeal and unilateral roll-call.
The Assembly title and tax resolution turn cohesion into a claim of sovereignty.

field_diffs.before: Church property is proposed as security for national debt; the question forces a conflict over corporate and private property.
field_diffs.after: Talleyrand proposes taking Church property, allocating two-thirds to support clergy after tithe loss and the rest to finance; Mirabeau instead demands national disposal of the whole with a general maintenance obligation. Debate pits trusteeship against institutional title and Declaration property rights, and market saturation against a loyal body of purchasers.

field_diffs.before: Deputies expect ecclesiastical reform; the source dates the national-property vote 3 November and explains state support obligations.
field_diffs.after: Prior reform convictions and hostile public galleries reinforce suspicion of clerical objections; no realistic debt alternative emerges. The source dates the vote 3 November, when 568 defeat 346 to place Church property at national disposal under Mirabeau’s broader formulation.

field_diffs.before: Borrowing and voluntary contribution fail to meet needs.
field_diffs.after: Necker’s political missteps and support for royal delay attract censure; failed August loans and the poorly yielding Patriotic Contribution cannot meet urgent needs.
